title: What is Kubernetes?
summary: What Kubernetes does, what it deliberately leaves out, and why containers led to it.

blocks.text: Welcome to the **Port of Kube**, a busy shipping port. Your apps are cargo, packed in standard shipping containers. Nobody here carries boxes by hand. You file an order like "always keep three containers of medicine on the water", and the port's crews make it happen and keep it true. Fittingly, **Kubernetes** is Greek for **helmsman**.

Kubernetes is an open source platform for running and managing **containerized workloads and services**. It is portable and extensible, and it supports both **declarative configuration** and automation.

items: The name comes from Greek for helmsman or pilot.
**K8s** is shorthand: there are eight letters between the "K" and the "s".
Google open sourced the project in 2014, building on its experience running production workloads at scale.

blocks.text: Declarative means you describe the state you want, and Kubernetes works to make the cluster match it.

Ships break down, crates go missing, and demand spikes before holidays. A good port handles that without the customer noticing: it swaps broken containers, spreads cargo across ships with spare room, and adds ships when orders pile up. Each row below is one of those port services.
In production something has to restart a crashed container, spread traffic and roll out new versions. Kubernetes provides a framework for running distributed systems resiliently.

rows: Expose containers by DNS name or IP and spread traffic across them
Mount storage of your choice: local, cloud provider, and more
Move actual state toward desired state at a controlled rate
Place containers on nodes based on the CPU and memory they need
Restart or replace failed containers; kill ones failing your health check
Update secrets and config without rebuilding images
Run batch and CI workloads, replacing failed containers if desired
Scale by command, UI, or automatically based on CPU usage
Allocate both address families to Pods and Services
Add features without changing upstream source code

blocks.text: The port moves and looks after containers. It does not run the factory that packs them (your build and CI/CD), and it does not sell you the goods inside (databases, caches, message buses). It hands you cranes, docks and rules, and lets you choose your own suppliers.
Kubernetes is **not a traditional, all-inclusive PaaS**. It works at the container level and gives you building blocks; the defaults it does ship are optional and pluggable.

items: It does not limit which kinds of applications you can run. If it runs in a container, it should run on Kubernetes.
It does not deploy source code or build your application. CI/CD is your choice.
It does not provide application-level services such as databases, message buses or caches as built-ins.
It does not dictate logging, monitoring or alerting solutions.
It does not provide or require a configuration language. It exposes a declarative API.
It does not provide full machine configuration, maintenance or management systems.

blocks.text: Kubernetes is not a step-by-step workflow engine ("do A, then B, then C"). It is a set of independent control processes that keep driving the current state toward the desired state.

sections.heading: From servers to VMs to containers

blocks.text: Shipping used to mean loose sacks thrown into one ship's hold, where a leaking barrel could ruin everyone's cargo (physical servers). Then every customer got a small ship of their own, carried inside a big one, with its own engine and crew (VMs). Then came the **standard container**: sealed boxes that share one ship's engine and crew, and fit any ship, truck or train (containers).

rows: No resource boundaries; one app could starve others
Several VMs per physical server, each with its own OS
Isolation and better utilization, but each VM is a full machine
Lightweight and portable across clouds and OS distributions

blocks.text: A container still has its own filesystem and its own share of CPU, memory and process space. Because it is decoupled from the infrastructure, the same image runs on a laptop and in the cloud.

items: Image immutability makes rollbacks quick and reliable.
Images are built at build/release time, not deploy time, which separates Dev and Ops concerns.
Apps are broken into smaller, independent pieces instead of one monolith on one big machine.

blocks.text: Every port has a **harbor office** that keeps the books and makes the decisions (the control plane), and a fleet of **cargo ships** that actually carry the containers (worker nodes). The table at the end of this section is your cast list for every story in this course.
A Kubernetes cluster is a **control plane** plus **one or more worker nodes**. The control plane manages the overall state of the cluster; node components keep Pods running.

items: Every node: `kubelet`, a container runtime, and optionally `kube-proxy`.
Addons extend the cluster, for example cluster DNS, the Dashboard web UI, resource monitoring and cluster-level logging.

blocks.title: An order moving through the Port of Kube

steps.text: You hand an order to the **front desk** (`kube-apiserver`). Every order and report goes through it.
The desk writes the order into the **ledger** (`etcd`), the record of what should exist.
The **load planner** (`kube-scheduler`) sees a new bay with no ship and picks a ship with room.
The **cargo officer** on that ship (`kubelet`) sees the assignment and has the **crane** (container runtime) load the containers into the **bay** (Pod).
The **supervisors** (`kube-controller-manager`) keep comparing the ledger with reality and fix any gap, such as a missing bay.

rows: The whole port: harbor office plus its fleet
The front desk: every order and report goes through it
The master ledger of what should exist
The load planner who picks a ship with room
Supervisors who compare the ledger with the docks and fix gaps

blocks.text: The Cluster Architecture topic covers each component in detail. Know which ones run on the control plane and which run on every node.

flashcards.front: What does "K8s" abbreviate, and why the 8?
flashcards.back: Kubernetes. There are eight letters between the "K" and the "s".

flashcards.front: What does the Greek root of "Kubernetes" mean?
Which company open sourced Kubernetes, and when?
Kubernetes manages what kind of workloads?

flashcards.back: It restarts or replaces failed containers, kills containers that fail your health check, and doesn't advertise them to clients until they're ready.
You tell Kubernetes how much CPU and memory each container needs, and it fits containers onto nodes to make the best use of resources.

flashcards.front: Does Kubernetes build your application from source?
flashcards.back: No. Building and deploying source code (CI/CD) is outside Kubernetes.

flashcards.front: Why does the Kubernetes overview say it is "not a mere orchestration system"?
flashcards.back: Instead of executing a fixed workflow (A, then B, then C), independent control processes continuously drive the current state toward the desired state.

flashcards.front: Key difference between a VM and a container?
flashcards.back: Each VM runs a full OS on virtualized hardware; containers share the host OS, so they are lighter.

flashcards.front: What are the two halves of every Kubernetes cluster?
flashcards.back: A control plane and one or more worker nodes.
kubelet, a container runtime, and kube-proxy (optional).

flashcards.front: How can you update secrets and app config in Kubernetes without rebuilding images?
flashcards.back: Use its secret and configuration management. You can deploy and update them without rebuilding container images.

options.text: A portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services
options.explanation: This matches the official overview: it manages containerized workloads and supports declarative configuration and automation.
Kubernetes does not build your application or deploy source code; that is left to your CI/CD tooling.

options.text: An all-inclusive Platform as a Service with a built-in database
options.explanation: The docs say it is not a traditional all-inclusive PaaS and does not provide databases as built-in services.
Kubernetes operates at the container level, not the hardware/VM level.

questions.stem: Where does the abbreviation "K8s" come from?

options.text: Eight letters between the "K" and the "s"
options.explanation: K-ubernete-s: the 8 replaces the eight letters in the middle.

options.text: Version 8 was the first public release
options.explanation: The abbreviation is about letter count, not a version number.

options.text: It runs on 8 nodes by default
options.explanation: There is no such default; a learning cluster can have a single node.
The name abbreviation has nothing to do with component count.

questions.stem: Which of these does Kubernetes provide? Select 3.

options.explanation: Listed feature: expose containers by DNS name or IP and load balance traffic.
Listed feature: change actual state to desired state at a controlled rate.
Listed feature: restarts, replaces and kills unhealthy containers.
Kubernetes explicitly does not provide or mandate a configuration language; it offers a declarative API.
Kubernetes does not build your application.

questions.stem: True or false: Kubernetes dictates which logging and monitoring solution you must use.

options.explanation: The overview says Kubernetes does not dictate logging, monitoring or alerting solutions.
Correct. It provides some integrations and mechanisms to export metrics, but the choice is yours.

questions.stem: Why does the overview say Kubernetes "eliminates the need for orchestration"?

options.text: Independent control processes continuously drive current state toward the desired state
options.explanation: Rather than running a fixed A→B→C workflow, control loops keep reconciling toward what you declared.

options.text: It runs a single central workflow engine
options.explanation: The docs say centralized control is not required.

options.text: It only runs one container per node
options.explanation: Unrelated, and not true: bin packing places many containers per node.

options.text: It hands orchestration to the cloud provider
options.explanation: Kubernetes runs on-premises and in clouds alike; this is not the reason.

questions.stem: What distinguishes containers from virtual machines, according to the overview?

options.text: Containers share the operating system among applications
options.explanation: Relaxed isolation that shares the OS is what makes containers lightweight.

options.text: Containers each run their own full operating system
options.explanation: That describes VMs.

options.text: Containers have no filesystem of their own
options.explanation: A container has its own filesystem, share of CPU, memory and process space.

options.text: Containers can only run on physical servers
options.explanation: Containers are portable across clouds and OS distributions.

questions.stem: What problem of the traditional deployment era did virtualization address?

options.text: No resource boundaries between applications on the same physical server
options.explanation: One app could take most resources; VMs isolate apps and improve utilization.
Containers came after virtualization in the timeline.
Not the problem described for that era.
Kubernetes did not exist in the traditional era.

questions.stem: True or false: Kubernetes can scale an application automatically based on CPU usage.

options.explanation: Horizontal scaling can be done by command, UI, or automatically based on CPU usage.
Automatic horizontal scaling based on CPU usage is a listed feature.

options.text: A control plane and one or more worker nodes
options.explanation: That is the definition on the Components page.

options.text: Only worker nodes that elect a leader
options.explanation: There is always a control plane managing cluster state.
Not required: the Components page only says a cluster has a control plane and one or more worker nodes.

options.text: An etcd database and a load balancer only
options.explanation: etcd is one control plane component; there are several more, plus nodes.

questions.stem: Which are things Kubernetes does NOT provide as built-in services? Select 2.

options.explanation: Application-level services like databases are not built in, though they can run on Kubernetes.
Middleware such as message buses is not built in.
That is self-healing, a core feature.
Load balancing is a core feature.

questions.stem: Which benefit of containers comes from image immutability?

options.explanation: The overview links reliable, frequent deployment with quick rollbacks to image immutability.
That is what VMs do, not container images.
Not related to immutability and not a Kubernetes built-in.
Images are built at build/release time by your tooling.

questions.stem: True or false: Kubernetes lets you add features to a cluster without changing upstream source code.

options.explanation: "Designed for extensibility" is one of the listed features.
Extensibility without upstream changes is an explicit design goal.
